tldr: By using a discrete masked diffusion model, SUAVE unifies language, video, and robot actions into a single vocabulary and a shared sequence. Changing which tokens to mask at inference turns this single foundation model into either a world model or a high-performance action policy.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of SUAVE. Language instructions, context video, target subgoal images, and action chunks are arranged in a single token sequence. A single masked diffusion transformer with block-causal attention denoises (reconstructs) future images and actions in parallel at the same time.
overview:
Recent robot learning has been driven by two major paradigms: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), which adapt vision-language foundation models for action prediction, and World Action Models (WAMs), which learn physical dynamics from video generation models. However, VLAs tend to act immediately without imagining the future, and they cannot learn from large amounts of action-free video. On the other hand, WAMs can imagine the future, but unifying their representations has been difficult because they use separate output heads for video and actions, or freeze language conditioning.

To address this, the authors developed SUAVE, an approach that unifies language, video frames, and robot actions into a single discrete vocabulary (token set) and models them simultaneously using a discrete masked diffusion transformer. Simply choosing which tokens to mask at inference time turns the exact same network weights into a world model (future video prediction), a robot policy (action generation), or a video-action model (joint future image and action generation). In addition, action-free human videos can be co-trained in the exact same batch and with the exact same loss as robot action data, simply by filling the action positions with mask tokens and excluding them from the loss calculation.

Evaluations on a real 7-DoF arm and multiple simulation benchmarks show that SUAVE is competitive with dedicated policies on static manipulation and outperforms all baselines on dynamic manipulation. Furthermore, on a real robot, it generates two subgoal images one second into the future and a 5-step action chunk in just 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU, sustaining closed-loop control at 2.5 Hz.
contributions: Proposed a framework that unifies language, video, and robot actions into a single discrete vocabulary, handling all three modalities simultaneously with a single transformer and a masked diffusion objective.

Achieved the flexibility to turn the same model weights into a world model, a policy, or a subgoal-conditioned action prediction model simply by changing which token positions are masked at inference time.

Introduced a mechanism to co-train action-free videos in the same batch by excluding masked action positions from the loss, demonstrating the effectiveness of pretraining and co-training with human videos.

Matched or exceeded the performance of dedicated world models and specialized action policies in both simulation and the real world, demonstrating real-robot closed-loop control at 2.5 Hz on an RTX 5090.

sections.heading: Beyond seeing and acting: Toward a unified model that imagines before acting
sections.summary: Conventional VLAs do not explicitly predict future observations, while WAMs separate video and action representations. This work uses discrete masked diffusion to represent language, video, and actions in a single shared sequence, rapidly generating future video and actions in parallel with just a few denoising steps.
sections.details:
Robot learning has recently shifted toward end-to-end training on large-scale datasets, driven by two paradigms: VLAs and WAMs.

However, because VLAs output actions directly from current observations, they do not explicitly predict what visual outcomes those actions will produce. Their inability to leverage action-free video data is another major drawback. On the other hand, WAMs can understand physical environment dynamics by predicting future video, but they operate in continuous latent spaces and often maintain separate output heads or representations for video and actions, falling short of true unification.

Recent work has shown the value of a "Visual Chain of Thought"—predicting intermediate subgoal images before acting. In other words, a capable policy should be able to imagine the future before it acts. However, doing this autoregressively (generating one token at a time) is too slow for real-time control on physical robots.

SUAVE solves this by adopting a discrete masked diffusion model. Because all tokens can be predicted in parallel, it can generate subgoal images and actions simultaneously in just a few denoising steps. Furthermore, simply altering which tokens are masked at inference turns the same set of weights into either a world model or a robot policy.

sections.heading: How SUAVE differs from existing VLAs and world models
sections.summary: This section reviews existing methods—such as autoregressive VLAs, continuous diffusion-based WAMs, and hybrid models—and positions SUAVE as a fourth design paradigm based on a single discrete vocabulary, a single masked diffusion objective, and parallel decoding.
sections.details:
Related work is organized across four perspectives:

### II-A Vision-language-action models
Some models, such as RT-2 and OpenVLA, discretize actions into tokens and predict them autoregressively, while others, like $\pi_{0}$, use flow matching (a form of continuous diffusion) in an action head. CoT-VLA predicts subgoal images before outputting actions, but token-by-token autoregressive generation slows down the control loop by a factor of seven.

### II-B World models and world action models
Video-generation-based world models such as Cosmos and iVideoGPT, as well as WAMs like DreamZero, have strong future prediction capabilities. However, they operate in continuous latent spaces, treat language as frozen conditioning from a pretrained encoder, and generate actions through separate heads, leaving these modalities disjointed.

### II-C Unified video-action and unified multimodal models
Prior attempts to jointly generate video and actions include UWM and UVA (continuous diffusion models) and UniVLA (discrete autoregressive tokens). SUAVE clearly distinguishes itself by placing language, video, and actions into a single discrete vocabulary, enabling cross-modal interactions through a single objective and parallel decoding.

### II-D Pretraining and co-training on video for robot policies
Existing ways to utilize action-free video include pretraining followed by fine-tuning (as in UniVLA) or maximizing diffusion noise during joint training (as in UWM). In discrete space, SUAVE co-trains on human video and robot demonstration data in a completely natural way: simply masking action positions and excluding them from the loss.

sections.heading: Architecture: Generating images and actions simultaneously with a single vocabulary and masked diffusion
sections.summary: Language, images (MAGViT-v2), and actions are concatenated into a shared token sequence with block-causal attention. The model is trained with cross-entropy loss by independently sampling mask ratios for video and actions, and achieves fast parallel inference using a Prefix KV cache.
sections.details:
The model architecture, training, and inference procedures of SUAVE are detailed below:

### III-B Tokenization and Sequence Layout
- Masked diffusion consists of a forward process that independently replaces clean tokens with a special mask token $[\mathrm{M}]$ with probability $t$, and a reverse process where a mask prediction network $p_{\theta}$ iteratively recovers the clean tokens. Because all tokens are predicted in parallel, the full sequence can be generated in few steps.

### III-B Tokenization and Sequence Layout
- Backbone: A 32-layer transformer based on the LLaDA architecture (MMaDA-8B), modified with a block-causal attention mask.
- Tokenizers: Language uses LLaDA; video uses MAGViT-v2 (converting 256×256 pixels into 16×16 = 256 discrete tokens, frozen weights); actions are uniformly discretized into 256 bins per dimension. All three modalities share a single token embedding table and output head.
- Sequence layout: Tokens are arranged in a single sequence: $[\mathtt{BOS}]$, language instruction, past context video frames (front and wrist views), target goal frames (front and wrist), and $K \times D$ future action chunk tokens.
- Block-causal attention: Attention is bidirectional within each block (e.g., within an image frame) and causal across blocks from past to future. This ensures action tokens attend to imagined future goal images during generation.

### III-C Training Objective
Mask ratios $r_v, r_a \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)$ are sampled independently for goal images and action tokens. The loss function is the average cross-entropy over masked positions. When training on action-free video (such as human manipulation video), the action block is filled with $[\mathrm{M}]$ and excluded from the loss calculation, allowing seamless co-training in the exact same batch.

### III-D Inference
At inference time, the model takes context video and language as input, and masks target positions depending on the desired mode. For robot control, the video-action mode is used (masking goal images and actions simultaneously). By caching Key-Value pairs for past conditioning tokens with a Prefix KV cache, 4 denoising steps generate one second of motion (front and wrist images plus a 5-step action chunk) in 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU. This speed sustains closed-loop control at roughly 2.5 Hz on a physical robot.

captions.F2: Token sequence layout and attention structure of SUAVE. The left shows the sequence of text, past context video, predicted goal images, and action chunks. As shown in the attention matrix on the right, attention is bidirectional within each block and causal across blocks, allowing actions to attend to imagined future images.

sections.heading: From real arms to simulators: Predictive power as a world model and strength as a policy
sections.summary: Evaluated on a physical xArm7, the static LIBERO benchmark, and the dynamic DOMINO benchmark. SUAVE matched dedicated Cosmos models in video prediction quality, outperformed baselines on dynamic manipulation as a policy, and demonstrated that video co-training significantly improves robustness to distribution shift.
sections.details:
The experiments investigated three questions: competitiveness against specialized policies (Q1), video prediction accuracy as a world model (Q2), and the benefits of video pretraining and co-training (Q3).

### IV-A Experimental Setup
Three variants were evaluated: "SUAVE-Scratch" (trained from scratch), "SUAVE-Pretrain" (pretrained on robot video), and "SUAVE-Cotrain" (pretrained with a 1:1 mix of robot video and Something-Something v2 human video). On a real 7-DoF xArm7, three tasks (vegetable picking, shoe organizing, and brush sweeping) were evaluated under nominal conditions and distribution-shifted conditions (unseen obstacles, unseen shoes, lighting changes).

- Real-robot results: Under nominal conditions, the average task score doubled from 0.31 for Scratch to 0.67 for Pretrain and 0.69 for Cotrain. Under distribution shift, while Scratch dropped sharply to 0.15, Pretrain maintained 0.49 and Cotrain reached 0.55—roughly three times higher.
- Video prediction accuracy: Compared to a dedicated Cosmos video model (2B parameters) trained on the same data, SUAVE achieved higher PSNR and competitive LPIPS. Qualitatively (Figure F4), while baselines suffered from spurious robot arm artifacts, incorrect arm positions, and severe color drift, SUAVE maintained consistent scene structure in its future rollouts.

### IV-B LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus for Static Manipulation
On the static manipulation benchmark LIBERO, SUAVE-Cotrain achieved an average success rate of 95.9%, leading LIBERO-Long tasks with 95.4%. In zero-shot evaluations on perturbed LIBERO-Plus, SUAVE-Cotrain achieved 71.3%, a 9.5-point gain over Scratch (61.8%), and achieved the highest accuracy of 82.5% under robot initial pose variations, surpassing $\pi_{0.5}$.

### IV-C DOMINO for Dynamic Manipulation
SUAVE's strengths were especially prominent on DOMINO, a dynamic benchmark involving moving objects. On the most challenging Level 3 setting where object velocities change discontinuously, SUAVE-Cotrain achieved an 8.2% success rate, with SUAVE-Scratch taking second place. While $\pi_{0.5}$ dropped to 1.7% despite leading on LIBERO, SUAVE's approach of imagining future images before acting proved remarkably effective in dynamic environments.

captions.F4: Comparison of long-horizon future video rollouts on real-robot tasks. While baseline methods (Cosmos, UniVLA, UVA, UWM) exhibit extra robot arm artifacts, positional errors, and severe color drift, SUAVE (red box) preserves accurate scene geometry and final states close to the ground truth (GT), aside from minor morphing in early frames.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future work: Unifying robot control and future prediction in a single model
sections.summary: The discrete masked diffusion model SUAVE confirms that real-robot closed-loop control, high-quality future video prediction, and strong dynamic manipulation capabilities can be achieved within a single set of weights. The authors also discuss limitations regarding tokenizer expressiveness and fixed sequence lengths.
sections.details:
SUAVE demonstrates that by unifying language, video, and actions into a single vocabulary and a masked diffusion transformer, the same network weights can seamlessly serve as a world model, an action policy, or a video-action model. Demonstrating real-time, simultaneous generation of subgoal images and action chunks on a physical robot is a significant practical milestone.

At the same time, the paper highlights several limitations:
- Human video co-training gains: Although co-training improved scores over pretraining alone, the performance differences were not statistically significant at the current data scale.
- Frozen tokenizer constraints: Because it uses a frozen MAGViT-v2 tokenizer, there is an upper bound on the visual reconstruction quality of generated frames.
- Fixed sequence length: The sequence length is fixed, meaning the model cannot dynamically adapt its generation horizon to task duration.
- Lack of language generation: Despite having a language model backbone, generating text itself and thoroughly evaluating linguistic generalization remain open challenges for future work.

takeaways: By using discrete masked diffusion, unified models that "imagine before acting" can perform parallel decoding, sustaining practical control rates (2.5 Hz) on real robots.

Simply changing which tokens are masked at inference allows a single-vocabulary architecture to flexibly switch between a video-predicting world model and an action-executing policy using the exact same weights.
Action-free video can be co-trained in the same batch with the same loss function simply by masking action positions, substantially boosting robustness to distribution shift.
Generating future subgoal images provides a significant advantage over specialized policies, particularly in dynamic manipulation tasks involving moving objects (such as the DOMINO benchmark).
limitations: At the current data scale, the performance advantage of human video co-training over robot video pretraining alone is not statistically significant.
Because the image tokenizer (MAGViT-v2) uses frozen weights, visual reconstruction artifacts such as early-frame morphing can occur in predicted images.
The token sequence length is fixed, meaning the model does not support variable-length prediction horizons tailored to task complexity or duration.
